p: The followers of the Mayamara Satra were predominantly Morans, the mainstay of the Ahom militia, joined by Sonowal Kacharis, Chutias, professional castes such as potters, weavers and fishermen, and some Ahom nobles and officers. The Ahom state rested on the Paik system, under which any able-bodied man who was not a Brahmin or a noble could be called up for labour, service or the army. The satras gave refuge to those seeking to escape it, and the loss of manpower brought them into growing conflict with the kingdom. The Mayamara Satra belonged to the non-conformist Kala-samhati sect, which competed with the royalist satras.

On 15 September 1769 Raghav Moran, a leading disciple of the satra, was flogged by Ahom officials for not supplying the required number of elephants. The Morans gathered an army of about seven thousand, and on 21 November 1769 they occupied the capital, imprisoned King Sunyeophaa and placed Ramakanta, son of the rebel leader Naharkhora, on the throne. After four months, when the peasant soldiers had gone home for the spring festival, nobles in disguise killed Raghav Moran on 14 April 1770 and retook the capital.

In April 1782 the Moamorias attacked the convoy of the newly crowned King Suhitpangphaa and briefly held Rangpur; the royalists who drove them out killed several thousand people. A third rising began in 1786. The rebels surrounded Rangpur in January 1788, the king left for Guwahati, and the continuous fighting in Upper Assam brought a famine described as the severest in the history of Assam. The rebels struck coins in the names of their leaders Bharat and Sarbananda but set up no central administration. A British contingent under Captain Welsh captured Rangpur in March 1794, but it was recalled and the rebels took the city again.

After the king's death Purnananda Burhagohain became the effective ruler and raised a standing army of paid sepoys in place of the paik militia. In 1805 his forces fought those of Sarbananda in the Bengmara region. Both sides recognised a stalemate, and Sarbananda accepted peace: he received the title of Barsenapati and autonomous command of the region, which came to be called the Matak rajya and paid annual tribute to the Ahom kingdom.

The population fell to about half of what it had been and economic life was disrupted. The paik and khel systems broke down, compelling the state to move towards a money economy. The weakened kingdom later fell to a Burmese invasion, which ultimately led to British colonisation.

notes: The article's dates are month-first; turned day-first.
The article spells the king of the second and third phases Suhitpangphaa, Suhutpanphaa and Gaurinath; I used Suhitpangphaa throughout and wrote 'the king's death' for Gaurinath's.
The rebel king appears as Bharat and Bhrarath (killed 1799); I used Bharat. The article is poorly edited in places; details of the many small engagements were left out.
